newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland backs convertible bonds in pension reform.
newsitem.headline: Poland backs convertible bonds in pension reform.

text.p: Poland's government on Tuesday initially approved a bill on issuing convertible bonds exchangeable into shares of privatised firms to finance the crucial reform of the country's social security system.

The bonds, with maturity of up to 10 years and open to both Polish and foreign investors, would help to boost privatisation revenues and finance the creation of new privately-managed pension funds, said Jerzy Hausner, the cabinet minister in charge of pension reform.
"The bill will combine privatisations of large, successful companies with the social security reform," he told a news conference after a cabinet meeting.
The government would now consult the draft law with trade unions and employers' groups and should give it a final approval and send to parliament later this month, Hausner said.
The draft is one of three crucial bills needed to trigger the long overdue pension system reform, which Hausner hopes will clear parliament in the next several months.

"This bill and bills on creating pension funds and on social insurance in industrial sectors should be approved before the summer holidays...if the pension reform is to take effect on January 1, 1999," he said.

Analysts and some politicians, including Labour Minister Tadeusz Zielinski, fear the campaign for parliamentary elections due around September will delay the passage of the reform plan well beyond 1997.

Many of Poland's nine million pensioners fear the reform would cut their benefits even though the government says their incomes are safe as long as the Polish economy continues to grow by at least five percent annually.

Hausner said the reform was urgent because the ageing of Polish society would lead to the collapse of public finances after 2004 if the current costly and inefficient pay-as-you-go system stays in place.

He said the pension reform would require increasing revenues from privatisation from the current one percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to two percent or about three billion zlotys ($965 million) annually.
Hausner said the bill on bonds would be accompanied by a list of companies whose shares would be available for the bonds.

He declined to give more details but later said that the telecom monopoly TPSA would make the list. "In my opinion a substantial stake in TPSA should be earmarked to support the pension reform," he said.
Government officials have earlier said the group of companies earmarked for the covertible bond scheme could also include distilleries and some banks.

The government is likely to earmark for the pension reform scheme about 30 percent of shares in companies slated for privatisation in 1997 and larger stakes of up to 65 percent, in firms which would be sold later, he said.

Proceeds from the bond sales would be pumped into a restructured state-run Social Security Office (ZUS), to make up for a loss of a part of premiums, which under the reform plan would be directed to new pension funds.

ZUS, now the sole pension provider, has to be subsidised by the central budget even though it gets 45 percent of all officially employed workers' wages. Subsidies to ZUS now account for 15 percent of budget spending.

Hausner said that under initial plans, 20 percent of the premium now paid to ZUS would go to new, privately-managed pension funds, which would be closely monitored by the government and would invest in low-risk securities and the convertible bonds.
People under 30 years of age at the time of the reform's launch would pay premiums to the new funds on a mandatory basis unless a different proposal was adopted.

Apart from pensions received from ZUS and from the new funds, people could secure extra benefits in fully private pension schemes by making voluntary contributions which the government is considering making tax deductible. ($ = 3.11 Polish Zlotys)
